sections.heading: The Short Answer
body: The easiest way to choose Indian takeaway in London is to avoid starting with a generic best-of list. Start by deciding whether the meal needs delivery or whether takeaway collection is acceptable, because that immediately changes the pool you should compare.

Once the service mode is clear, narrow the shortlist by cuisine style, review depth, and local area strength. That gives a faster and more reusable framework than scanning one long list of famous restaurants.

sections.heading: Why Service Fit Comes Before Prestige
body: Takeaway intent is different from dine-in intent. A famous dining room can still be the wrong answer if the listing does not match the way you actually want to get the food, while a less famous local option can be a better fit for a weeknight order because the service mode is clearer and the proof is stronger for home use.

The current directory supports that distinction because delivery appears on 1,770 Indian-labelled listings and takeaway appears on 1,886. Readers do not need to begin with editorial prestige when the service data already narrows the field so quickly.

sections.heading: Delivery And Takeaway Are Similar, But Not The Same Search
body: Delivery-first readers usually care most about convenience, travel distance, and whether the order still feels dependable when it arrives at home. Takeaway-first readers can accept collection, which often gives them a slightly larger pool and more flexibility when browsing by area.

In the current dataset, 1,754 Indian-labelled listings support both delivery and takeaway, so the overlap is large. That means the smartest workflow is not to treat them as separate worlds, but to decide which mode matters most and then keep the other as a fallback.

sections.heading: Use Cuisine Style Before Ratings
body: Ratings matter, but they should come after style fit. A reader who wants dosa, idli, and rice-led dishes is solving a different problem from someone who wants tandoor items, naan, paneer, or richer curry-house mains, so the first comparison should be menu direction rather than score alone.

This matters even more for home ordering because menu style strongly affects what feels satisfying outside the restaurant. The service page helps with delivery or takeaway intent, but category and menu cues still decide whether the order matches the meal you had in mind.

sections.heading: What The London Directory Currently Shows
body: The local evidence is strong enough to support filtering. The project currently holds 1,983 Indian-labelled listings, including 1,770 with delivery signals, 1,886 with takeaway signals, and 731 delivery-friendly listings rated 4.5 or higher. That is a large enough pool to choose by fit rather than by one editorial ranking.

The proof depth is also meaningful. The takeaway subset includes 1,463 listings with at least 100 reviews, and the delivery subset carries a combined visible review footprint of 1,393,242. In practical terms, readers can filter aggressively for service mode without running out of restaurants that still have strong public proof.

sections.heading: Local Area Still Changes The Quality Of The Shortlist
body: Takeaway intent is still local intent. Harrow currently leads the delivery pool with 110 listings and the takeaway pool with 117, while Newham, Hounslow, Brent, Tower Hamlets, Ealing, Hillingdon, and Westminster also show deep service-ready pools. That means some boroughs let readers stay very specific, while others may need a wider search radius.

A practical workflow is to choose service mode first, then move into borough or area browsing only if the shortlist still feels too long. This keeps the search grounded in the meal need instead of forcing location to do all the work.

sections.heading: How To Make The Final Takeaway Decision
body: Once the shortlist is small, compare the rating together with the review count, then check whether the style of food still looks right for home ordering. A slightly lower score backed by substantial proof is often safer than a newer listing with almost no review depth.

After that, use the directory details the same way you would for any other decision: confirm the area, the service options, and whether the listing gives enough confidence to order. The goal is not to find the single best Indian takeaway in London for everyone, but the best-fit option for this specific order.

faqs.question: What should I check first when choosing Indian takeaway in London?
faqs.answer: Check whether you need delivery or whether takeaway collection is acceptable. That first filter cuts down the shortlist faster than starting with ratings alone.

faqs.question: Is takeaway broader than delivery in the current directory?
faqs.answer: Yes. The current dataset shows 1,886 Indian-labelled listings with takeaway signals and 1,770 with delivery signals, so takeaway currently covers a slightly larger pool.

faqs.question: Should I choose by rating or by cuisine style first?
faqs.answer: Choose by cuisine style first, then use rating and review volume to make the final decision. Style decides whether the meal matches what you actually want; proof decides whether the restaurant looks dependable.

faqs.question: Which London areas currently have strong Indian takeaway pools?
faqs.answer: Harrow is the strongest current pool in this dataset, with Newham, Hounslow, Brent, Tower Hamlets, Ealing, Hillingdon, and Westminster also showing deep service-ready coverage.

faqs.question: Can I use the same framework for other restaurant directories?
faqs.answer: Yes. This is a reusable service-intent framework: choose service mode first, narrow by cuisine style, compare proof, then use area to make the final shortlist manageable.
